newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cautious Blair keeps options open in France.
newsitem.headline: Cautious Blair keeps options open in France.

text.p: With a caution virtually indistinguishable from Prime Minister John Major's, British opposition leader Tony Blair told France on Friday he would keep London's options open on joining a single European currency.
Blair promised a more constructive relationship with the European Union than Major's fractious Conservatives if his Labour Party wins a general election due by next May.
But he left President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe little wiser on whether Britain under Labour would join EU economic and monetary union or not.
"What is important to recognise is that the options should be kept open, but the test is Britain's national economic interest," he told reporters after an hour of talks with Chirac.

"Should we participate in a single currency, that has to be done with the full consent of the British people," Blair said. "Unless it is the issue at a general election, then there must be a referendum."
Labour has a big lead over the Conservatives in opinion polls, but surveys also show a single currency is deeply unpopular with voters, except among British business leaders.
Against that background, Blair carefully set out the pros and cons of monetary union while hinting at a preference for joining.

In a speech to French businessmen, he said: "In principle we can see advantages in favour of a single currency -- stability in exchange rates and lower interest rates -- and we have also made it clear that, unlike the Conservatives, there is no insuperable constitutional or political objection."

But he went on to say: "We will need convincing that the economic conditions will allow it to succeed. For a currency union between nations to work there needs to be genuine and sustainable convergence in the way their economies perform and in the way they react to external shocks.

"Otherwise, with exchange rate adjustments no longer possible and only limited scope for adjustment through labour migration or fiscal transfers, the risks of countries finding themselves saddled with the wrong policies are too great."
Blair told Chirac, a socially minded Gaullist who does not share Major's zeal for deregulation, of his vision of a "third way" between bureaucratic over-regulation and laisser-faire economic policy.

In contrast to Major, who has vowed to overturn an EU directive setting a maximum 48-hour work week, which the European Court of Justice this week ordered Britain to obey, Blair said he believed the rule was "right on the merits".

But he also said he favoured labour market flexibility once minimum standards had been achieved and would not allow the European Union to legislate by majority voting on social security or workers' co-determination in industry.
He pointedly declined to endorse the French Socialist party's decision last weekend to demand a 35-hour work week with no loss of earnings in its 1998 election manifesto.

Refusing direct comment on the plan in the name of diplomacy, Blair said a choice by workers to work shorter hours might help to reduce unemployment but added: "You've got to balance out the economic questions."

Blair sought to play down the whole issue of the Maastricht treaty's social chapter, from which Britain under Major opted out, saying there was "no appetite amongst other governments in Europe for vast new amounts of labour market regulation".
French officials declined to comment on their impressions of Blair, citing the sensitive pre-election period in Britain.
The opposition leader sought to convince businessmen that Labour would wield greater influence in defending British interests in Europe because it would behave more constructively.
"The issue for Britain should not be 'in or out'. We are in to stay. Once that is accepted, the futility of being at the margins of influence is surely plain," he said.
